Course Description 
Students interested in careers in travel, hospitality, event planning, or any aspect of the tourism 
industry. This course is also ideal for those who love exploring different cultures and places. The 
Exploring the World of Tourism course offers students an exciting introduction to the dynamic 
and diverse field of tourism. This course is designed to ignite a passion for travel and hospitality, 
providing students with a broad understanding of the tourism industry, including its history, 
development, and current trends. Students create and evaluate local, national or international tour 
packages, including itinerary, cost and attractions information, and traveller information. 
 
 
Course Objectives 
• To understand the significance and impact of tourism on local, national, and global 
economies and culture. 
• To explore various sectors within the tourism industry such as hospitality, travel services, 
event planning, accommodations, and destination marketing. 
• To develop key skills in customer service, communication, professionalism, and cultural 
sensitivity, essential for a successful career in tourism. 
• To analyze the role of sustainable and responsible tourism in preserving cultural, 
environmental, and natural heritage. 
• To gain practical insights through case studies analysis, conversations, and industry 
professionals. 
 
 
Units of Study 
Students will explore and research Travel Services, Hospitality Management, Event and 
Recreation Management, Cultural and Eco-Tourism, Tourism Marketing and Promotion, 
Accommodations, Surface and Air Transportation, Potential Career Opportunities in Tourism.

The Canadian tourism sector is a vital part of the country's economy and culture, known for its 
diverse landscapes, rich history, and vibrant cities. Here is an overview of the Canadian tourism 
sector: 
 
Natural Beauty: Canada is renowned for its stunning natural beauty, including pristine 
wilderness areas, vast forests, majestic mountains, and thousands of lakes and rivers. Iconic 
attractions like Banff and Jasper National Parks in the Canadian Rockies, Niagara Falls, and the 
rugged coastline of British Columbia draw millions of visitors each year. 
 
Cultural Diversity: Canada's multicultural society is reflected in its tourism offerings. Visitors 
can experience a wide range of cultural events, festivals, and cuisines from around the world. 
Major cities like Toronto, Vancouver, and Montreal are hubs of cultural diversity and offer a 
variety of attractions, museums, and vibrant neighborhoods. 
 
Outdoor Activities: Canada offers numerous outdoor activities year-round. In the winter, 
visitors can enjoy skiing and snowboarding in places like Whistler, while the summer offers 
opportunities for hiking, biking, and water sports. Canada is also known for its excellent fishing, 
wildlife watching, and camping options. 
 
Indigenous Tourism: Canada has a rich Indigenous heritage, and Indigenous tourism has been 
growing in popularity. Visitors can learn about Indigenous cultures, traditions, and art through 
experiences such as guided tours, art galleries, and cultural festivals. 
 
Eco-Tourism: Sustainability and eco-tourism are increasingly important in Canada. Many 
tourists seek eco-friendly and responsible travel options, and Canada's commitment to preserving 
its natural beauty aligns with these values. There are eco-lodges, wildlife sanctuaries, and 
conservation projects throughout the country. 
 
Historical Sites: Canada has a rich history, with numerous historic sites and landmarks. Visitors 
can explore places like Old Quebec City, the historic district of Halifax, and the well-preserved 
forts and trading posts of the fur trade era. 
 
Adventure Tourism: Canada is a haven for adventure enthusiasts. Activities such as white-
water rafting, ziplining, rock climbing, and dog sledding attract thrill-seekers from around the 
world. 
 
Urban Attractions: Canada's major cities offer a wide range of attractions, including world-
class restaurants, shopping, theater, and sports events. Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal, Ottawa, 
and Calgary are some of the most popular urban destinations.

Events and Festivals: Canada hosts numerous events and festivals throughout the year, 
celebrating everything from music and film to food and culture. Examples include the Toronto 
International Film Festival, Calgary Stampede, and Quebec Winter Carnival. 
 
Accessibility: Canada is easily accessible to international visitors with major airports in cities 
across the country. The country also has a well-developed transportation network, including 
trains and buses, making it convenient for tourists to explore different regions. 
 
The Canadian government, along with provincial and territorial authorities, actively promotes 
tourism and works to enhance the visitor experience. The tourism sector contributes significantly 
to the Canadian economy and plays a crucial role in showcasing the country's diversity. 
 
Travel motivators and trends are dynamic and can change over time as societal, economic, and 
technological factors evolve. Here are some common travel motivators and trends that have been 
observed in recent years: 
 
Travel Motivators: 
• Relaxation and Stress Relief: Many people seek travel as a way to unwind, de-stress, 
and escape the demands of daily life. Relaxing on a beach, staying at a spa resort, or 
practicing mindfulness in a natural setting are common motivations for travel. 
• Exploration and Adventure: Some travelers are motivated by a desire to explore new 
destinations, embark on adventures, and experience different cultures. Activities like 
hiking, wildlife safaris, and exploring remote destinations are popular choices. 
• Cultural Immersion: Travelers often seek authentic cultural experiences, including 
trying local cuisine, participating in cultural festivals, and interacting with local 
communities. Cultural immersion can provide a deeper understanding of a destination. 
• Family and Friends: Visiting friends and family is a significant motivator for travel. 
Reconnecting with loved ones, attending family events, and spending quality time 
together drive many trips. 
• Bucket List Experiences: Travelers may have specific destinations or experiences 
they've always dreamed of, such as seeing the Northern Lights, visiting iconic landmarks 
like the Eiffel Tower, or attending major sporting events. 
• Wellness and Health Tourism: Wellness tourism is on the rise, with travelers seeking 
destinations that offer opportunities for fitness, relaxation, and holistic well-being. This 
includes spa retreats, yoga and meditation retreats, and wellness-focused resorts. 
• Educational and Learning Experiences: Travelers increasingly opt for educational 
trips, such as language immersion programs, cooking classes, or cultural workshops, to 
acquire new skills and knowledge. 
• Sustainable and Eco-Friendly Travel: Concerns about environmental conservation and 
sustainability are driving a growing trend in eco-tourism. Travelers are seeking 
destinations and accommodations that prioritize eco-friendly practices. 
 
Travel Trends: 
• Digital Nomadism: The rise of remote work has given birth to the digital nomad trend, 
where individuals work while traveling. Many are choosing to live and work in different 
destinations, often for extended periods.

In guest service and hospitality, there are several fundamental competencies that professionals 
should possess to provide excellent service and ensure a positive experience for guests. These 
competencies include: 
 
Positive Attitude: A positive attitude is essential in the hospitality industry. It involves being 
friendly, approachable, and enthusiastic when interacting with guests. A positive demeanor can 
create a welcoming and comfortable atmosphere for guests. 
 
Responsibility: Responsibility in guest service means taking ownership of one's duties and 
obligations. This includes being punctual, reliable, and accountable for tasks and commitments. 
It also involves handling guest requests and concerns promptly and effectively. 
 
Adaptability: The hospitality industry is dynamic and often requires professionals to adapt to 
changing circumstances, such as guest preferences, special requests, or unexpected situations. 
Being adaptable means being flexible and open to adjusting to meet the needs of guests. 
 
Willingness to Continuously Learn: The hospitality industry is constantly evolving, with new 
trends, technologies, and guest expectations emerging. Professionals in this field should have a

Description: Students research and discuss issues related to alternative accommodations. 
 
Alternative accommodations offer travelers a diverse range of options beyond traditional hotels 
and resorts. These accommodations provide unique experiences and cater to various preferences 
and interests. Here are descriptions of different types of alternative accommodations: 
 
Boutique Hotels: Boutique hotels are small, independently owned hotels known for their 
distinctive character, design, and personalized service. They often have a specific theme or style, 
and their intimate atmosphere appeals to travelers seeking a unique and intimate experience. 
 
Specialty Hotels: Specialty hotels focus on a particular theme or niche market. Examples 
include wellness retreats, art-themed hotels, wine resorts, and historical landmarks converted into 
accommodations. These hotels provide immersive experiences aligned with their chosen theme. 
 
Bed and Breakfast (B&B): B&Bs are typically small, family-run properties that offer cozy 
rooms and a homey atmosphere. Guests are provided with breakfast as part of their stay and 
often have the opportunity to interact with the hosts, creating a personalized experience. 
 
Guest Ranch: Guest ranches, also known as dude ranches, offer guests the chance to experience 
life on a working ranch. Visitors can participate in activities like horseback riding, cattle herding, 
and outdoor adventures while enjoying comfortable accommodations. 
 
Country Vacation Rentals: Country vacation rentals are self-catering properties located in rural 
or countryside settings. These can include cottages, farmhouses, and rural cabins, providing a 
peaceful escape for guests seeking a quiet retreat. 
 
Full-Service Lodge: Full-service lodges are often situated in natural settings, such as national 
parks or wilderness areas. They offer comfortable accommodations, dining options, and various 
recreational activities like hiking, fishing, and wildlife watching. 
 
Basic Cabin Lodge: Basic cabin lodges provide simple, rustic accommodations in remote or 
wilderness locations. These are ideal for guests looking to disconnect from modern amenities and 
immerse themselves in nature. 
 
Eco-Lodge: Eco-lodges are environmentally responsible accommodations designed to minimize 
their impact on the environment. They often use sustainable practices, incorporate renewable 
energy sources, and provide educational opportunities about conservation. 
 
Camp or Campground: Camps and campgrounds offer outdoor enthusiasts the chance to stay 
in tents or RVs in natural settings. These accommodations are ideal for camping enthusiasts who 
want to experience the great outdoors.

shared facilities, catering to backpackers and budget-conscious travelers. Some hostels also offer

The economic impact of alternative accommodations on the tourism industry has been significant 
and has contributed to both opportunities and challenges. Alternative accommodation influences 
the tourism industry economically: 
 
• Increased Market Competition: Alternative accommodations have intensified 
competition in the tourism sector. With a wider range of options available, traditional 
hotels and resorts are challenged to improve their services, pricing, and marketing 
strategies to remain competitive. 
 
• Revenue Diversification: Alternative accommodations provide additional sources of 
revenue for property owners and local economies. Many homeowners and property 
investors have turned to platforms like Airbnb to rent out spare rooms or entire 
properties, generating income from tourism. 
 
• Expansion of Tourism Demand: Alternative accommodations have broadened the 
appeal of travel by offering unique and immersive experiences. This expansion of options 
can attract new segments of travelers who might not have considered traditional hotels, 
contributing to overall industry growth. 
 
• Local Economic Impact: Stays in alternative accommodations often benefit local 
businesses. Travelers who stay in vacation rentals may shop at nearby markets, dine in 
local restaurants, and participate in local activities, stimulating the local economy. 
 
• Job Creation: The rise of alternative accommodations has led to the creation of jobs in 
various areas, including property management, cleaning services, maintenance, and guest 
services. These jobs provide employment opportunities in communities where these 
accommodations are located. 
 
• Tax Revenue: Many cities and municipalities have implemented taxes and fees on 
alternative accommodations, similar to those imposed on traditional hotels. These taxes

While they offer numerous benefits, they also present challenges related to regulation and market 
dynamics.  
 
Owning and operating an alternative accommodation facility, such as a vacation rental, 
guesthouse, or bed and breakfast, can offer various advantages and disadvantages. The decision 
to pursue such an endeavor should take into account these factors: 
 
Advantages: 
• Income Generation: One of the primary advantages is the potential for income 
generation. Renting out your property can provide a steady stream of revenue, making it a 
profitable investment. 
• Flexibility and Control: As the owner, you have greater control over the property, 
allowing you to set rental rates, establish house rules, and manage availability based on 
your preferences. 
• Tax Benefits: There may be tax benefits associated with owning an alternative 
accommodation, such as deducting expenses related to maintenance, utilities, and 
property management. 
• Diversified Portfolio: Investing in alternative accommodations can diversify your real 
estate portfolio and reduce reliance on traditional rental properties. 
• Personal Use: Depending on the property's availability, you may have the option to use it 
for personal vacations or getaways when it's not rented out. 
• Creativity and Personalization: You can infuse your personality and style into the 
property, creating a unique and personalized experience for guests.

• Regulatory Challenges: Depending on your location, there may be regulatory hurdles to

impact the use of your property. 
• Competition: The growth of the alternative accommodation industry has increased

The concept of a tourist destination life cycle is a useful tool for understanding the evolution of a

Exploration Stage:

Involvement Stage: 
• Local residents provide some services to tourists, often in a small and informal way.

Development Stage:

• Marketing efforts increase to attract more tourists. 
• The destination’s economy becomes increasingly dependent on tourism. 
• Local involvement and control in tourism begin to diminish, external companies step-in. 
 
Consolidation Stage: 
• Tourism becomes a significant part of the destination’s economy. 
• The number of tourists continues to grow, potentially leading to overcrowding. 
• The destination may lose some of its original charm and character, impacting the quality 
of the visitor experience. 
• Conflicts arise between residents and tourists due to overcrowding and resource strain. 
 
Stagnation Stage: 
• The destination reaches its peak in terms of visitor numbers. 
• Infrastructure may be outdated, and the environment may be degraded due to overuse. 
• The destination becomes less appealing, and a decline in tourist numbers may begin. 
• Marketing becomes more challenging as the destination's image may be perceived as less 
attractive. 
 
Post-Stagnation Stage: 
• Decline: Without renewal or reinvention, the destination may face a decline. Tourists 
might be replaced by different visitor types (such as budget travelers), leading to changes

offerings, upgrading infrastructure, and rebranding. This can attract new types of tourists 
and open new markets, leading to a resurgence in popularity. 
 
It's important to note that not all destinations will necessarily go through each of these stages

The economic impact of destination development in tourism is multifaceted, involving various 
aspects such as the multiplier effect, revenue leakage, and balance of payments. These factors in 
understanding how tourism development can affect a country's economy: 
 
Multiplier Effect: 
• The multiplier effect in tourism refers to how spending by tourists circulates through a 
destination’s economy. Money spent at a destination is re-spent in the local economy in 
various forms, such as salaries for employees, purchases from local suppliers, and 
investments in local infrastructure. 
• This effect can significantly boost local economies. For instance, when a hotel employs 
local staff, those employees spend their income locally, which further stimulates other 
sectors of the economy. 
• The strength of the multiplier effect depends on the capacity of the local economy to 
retain and re-circulate the tourist spending. If the local economy has a diverse range of 
businesses and services, the multiplier effect is likely to be higher. 
 
Revenue Leakage: 
• Revenue leakage occurs when the income generated by tourism is lost to other 
economies. This happens when a portion of tourism revenue is not retained locally. 
• Common causes of revenue leakage include the import of goods and services to meet 
tourists' needs, foreign ownership of tourism businesses, and marketing and promotion 
expenses paid to companies outside the destination. 
• For instance, if a hotel is owned by a foreign company, a substantial portion of the 
income generated may be sent back to the company’s home country rather than being 
reinvested in the local economy. If tourists predominantly use international tour 
operators, a significant part of their spending may never reach the destination’s economy. 
 
Balance of Payments: 
• Tourism affects a country’s balance of payments, which is a record of all economic 
transactions between residents of that country and the rest of the world.

• Tourism can be a significant source of foreign exchange earnings, which can help 
improve a country's balance of payments. When tourists visit a country, they bring in 
foreign currency, which is then exchanged for currency to pay for goods and services. 
• If a country relies heavily on imports for its tourism sector or there's significant revenue 
leakage, the potential positive impact on the balance of payments can be diminished.

The history and development of passenger rail travel in Canada is a fascinating journey that 
reflects the nation's growth and changing transportation needs. Canada's vast distances and 
diverse geography have played a significant role in shaping its railway system. An overview: 
 
1. Early Development (19th Century): 
• Beginnings: Canada's passenger rail history began in the early 19th century. The 
first public railway, the Champlain and Saint Lawrence Railroad, opened in 1836. 
It was primarily for freight, but it also marked the beginning of passenger rail 
service. 
• Expansion: With Confederation in 1867, railway expansion became a national 
priority, essential for linking distant communities and facilitating trade. The 
Canadian Pacific Railway (CPR) was established in 1881 and played a crucial 
role in connecting the country from coast to coast, with its transcontinental line 
completed in 1885. 
 
2. Golden Age (Early 20th Century): 
• Peak of Rail Travel: The early 20th century can be considered the golden age of 
passenger rail travel in Canada. Luxurious transcontinental trains like the 
Canadian Pacific’s “Canadian” and the Canadian National Railway's (CNR) 
“Super Continental” offered elegant travel experiences. 
• Nation Building: Railways were instrumental in nation-building, facilitating 
immigration and settlement in the West and fostering national unity. 
 
3. Mid-20th Century Challenges: 
• Competition from Cars and Planes: With the advent of the automobile and the 
airline industry's growth in the mid-20th century, passenger rail began to face stiff 
competition. 
• Decline in Popularity: The convenience of cars and the speed of air travel led to 
a decline in passenger rail's popularity, resulting in reduced services and the 
discontinuation of some routes. 
 
4. Establishment of VIA Rail (1970s): 
• In response to declining passenger rail services and the financial struggles of CNR 
and CPR in providing these services, the Canadian government established VIA 
Rail in 1978 as a Crown corporation.

maintaining essential intercity passenger rail services across the country.

• Continued Challenges and Innovations: Despite ongoing challenges, including 
funding and competition from other modes of transport, VIA Rail has continued

The development of the cruise industry is a fascinating journey marked by evolution and 
innovation. It has transformed from a mode of transportation to a significant segment of the 
leisure travel industry. An overview of its development: 
 
1. Early Days (Late 19th - Early 20th Century): 
• Originally, ocean liners were primarily used for transporting passengers and cargo 
across seas and oceans. These journeys were often long and uncomfortable, 
mainly serving the purpose of migration and trade. 
• The concept of cruising for pleasure began in the late 19th century. Companies 
like the Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Company (P&O) started 
offering pleasure voyages to destinations like the Mediterranean, catering to 
Europe’s wealthy elite. 
 
2. The Golden Age of Ocean Liners (1920s-1950s): 
• This era saw the rise of luxurious ocean liners like the RMS Titanic, Queen Mary, 
and Queen Elizabeth. These ships were symbols of national prestige and 
technological advancement. 
• While primarily used for transatlantic voyages, these liners offered increasingly 
luxurious accommodations and amenities, attracting wealthy travelers. 
 
3. Transformation and Growth (1960s-1980s): 
• The advent of affordable and faster air travel in the 1960s led to a decline in ocean 
liner travel. In response, the industry shifted its focus from transportation to 
leisure-oriented cruising. 
• Companies like Norwegian Caribbean Lines (now Norwegian Cruise Line) 
pioneered the concept of Caribbean cruises. This saw the introduction of ships 
designed specifically for cruising, offering various activities and entertainment. 
 
4. Modern Cruise Industry (1990s-Present): 
• The modern era of cruising is characterized by massive growth and 
diversification. Cruise ships have become destinations in themselves, offering an 
array of amenities like multiple dining options, theaters, pools, spas, and even 
theme park-like attractions.

price points and to an array of destinations around the world, including the

in terms of size and onboard offerings. 
 
5. Innovation and Sustainability:

environmental sustainability, energy efficiency, and reducing carbon footprint. 
• The industry is also exploring new technologies like LNG-powered ships and

overcrowding in tourist destinations, and, more recently, the impact of the 
COVID-19 pandemic.

stringent health and safety protocols and continuing to innovate and adapt to 
changing travel trends. 
 
The cruise industry has evolved from a means of transportation to a comprehensive leisure

Auto and recreational vehicle (RV) travel offer a range of options for travelers, each catering to 
different styles of road trips and experiences. Here’s a breakdown of the various types available: 
 
1. Automobile Travel: 
• Personal Cars: The most common form of auto travel, personal cars offer 
flexibility and convenience for both short and long journeys. They are ideal for 
family road trips, weekend getaways, and exploring off-the-beaten-path 
destinations. 
• Rental Cars: For travelers who don't own a car or are visiting, rental cars provide 
an accessible option for road travel. Rental agencies offer a range of vehicles to 
suit different needs, from economy cars to luxury vehicles. 
• Car Sharing Services: Services like Zipcar allow travelers to rent cars for short 
periods, often by the hour, providing a flexible and cost-effective option for urban 
travelers or those needing a car for a brief period. 
 
2. Recreational Vehicle (RV) Travel: 
• Motorhomes: These are self-contained units where the living quarters are part of 
the vehicle. They come in various sizes: 
• Class A: Large and luxurious, resembling buses. 
• Class B: Smaller and more van-like, often called camper vans. 
• Class C: Mid-sized, built on a truck chassis with over-cab sleeping area. 
• Travel Trailers: These are towed behind a vehicle and come in various sizes and 
designs, from lightweight teardrop trailers to large, family-sized travel trailers.

• Truck Campers: A camper that can be loaded onto the bed of a pickup truck,

3. Specialized Recreational Vehicles:

remote locations.

• High-end motorhomes offering the comforts and amenities of a home, such as full 
kitchens, bathrooms, entertainment systems, and spacious living areas. They cater 
to travelers seeking a luxurious road travel experience. 
 
Each type of auto and RV travel offers unique experiences and caters to different travel needs, 
from simple and rugged to luxurious and comprehensive.

repack is a major draw.

buffet restaurants, formal dining rooms, and specialty restaurants offering cuisines

• Inter-city Travel: Amtrak, the national passenger railroad service, provides inter-city

• Tourism and Scenic Journeys: Similar to Canada, certain train routes in the U.S., like the

tourists looking for a unique travel experience.

transportation, which is becoming increasingly important in the context of climate 
change. They also provide an accessible travel option for people who cannot drive or 
prefer not to fly.
